title: Deciphering Growth Kinetics of a Topological Insulator using in-situ 4D-STEM
content: In-situ four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy (4D-STEM) can be used to understand the dynamics of the crystallization processes that materials undergo in order to reveal, and eventually utilize, unique metastable states. This is of particular interest during the re-crystallization process found in the topological insulator, Bi2Se3 [1-2]. Bi2Se3 was recently discovered to undergo out-of-equilibrium crystallization during atomic resolution STEM through electron beam-induced interactions. Through the controlled use of the electron beam, the crystallization of this material from the amorphous phase can be induced while simultaneously allowing for the direct capture of the growth dynamics. This is done through the use of in-situ 4D-STEM datasets which consist of a stack of convergent beam electron diffraction (CBED) patterns acquired across the 2D surface taken over time [4]. These datasets can then be used to elucidate the science that links growth parameters and the different thermodynamic and non-thermodynamic routes to convert MBE-grown amorphous Bi-Se films to stable and metastable polymorphs of Bi2Se3. For these experiments, a Dectris direct electron detector was utilized, thus allowing accurate data acquisition with dwell times of only several milliseconds per acquired pattern. Using this technique, we were able to gather information over what types of crystalline domains form, their respective size, and the orientations they grow in as a result of the electron beam irradiation.
